subject: Meridian pilot sizing: performance & safety matrix for dedicated slabs
messages:

Subject: Pilot sizing ask — real-time triage (tokens/sec + headroom)

Ben,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Meridian is moving quickly — procurement asked us for a simple sizing packet for the pilot so we can scope committed capacity. High level requirements below:

- Primary workload: clinical triage assistant for incoming patient messages. Mostly short prompts (average 120 tokens request, 80 tokens response).
- Peak bursts observed in internal load tests: up to ~12k tokens/sec sustained for ~5–10min, with rare spikes to 18k tps for <1min.
- P95 latency target: <= 350ms for user-facing calls (goal).
- Model: prefer an open Llama-variant you support with int8 quantization; we can evaluate both high-throughput and latency-sensitive variants.
- Must show required reserved capacity (slabs / GPUs) to meet SLO with 1.5x safety margin and note fallback options.

Attached is a short FAQ and the pilot scope doc. Can you send a short matrix showing tokens/sec -> slab count -> expected p95? Also call out any recommended config (KV cache, batching, quantization) and an ops playbook for warmup.

Appreciate a quick turnaround — procurement wants this for their upcoming committee on Friday.

Cheers,
Laurent
Principal Product Manager
Meridian Health

Subject: Re: Pilot sizing ask — real-time triage (tokens/sec + headroom)

Laurent — thanks for the clear requirements. Looping in Monica (CS) and Priyom (inference infra) for numbers + operational notes. High-level summary below so your procurement committee has something concise. Full worksheet attached ("meridian_sla_workbook.xlsx").

TL;DR recommendation
- Recommended reserved: 8 dedicated A100-80GB equivalent slabs (can be H100 if you prioritize lower latency) for baseline pilot commit.
- Expected sustained capacity: ~14k tokens/sec with auto-burst headroom to ~20k tps for short spikes when using aggressive prefix caching + int8 fused kernels.
- Estimated p95 latency (120+80 tokens avg) with 1.5x safety margin: ~280–360 ms depending on model variant and network egress.

Assumptions used in the matrix:
- Model family: LLaMA-3-13B optimized kernel path; int8 quantization with per-channel scales.
- Avg sequence processed per request: 200 tokens (120 in + 80 out).
- KV cache hit rate: 45% (conservative for triage with reused context across conversations).
- Batching window: 20–30ms for latency-sensitive path; continuous batching engaged for background throughput.

Why 8 slabs?
- Baseline compute mapping targets p95 <= 350ms at 12k sustained tps. Each A100-80GB equivalent slab (advertised as a "slab" in our committed capacity product) supports ~1.8k–2.0k tps in this workload when using int8 kernels and KV caching.
- 8 slabs -> ~14.4–16k nominal tps; with autoscaling + urgent-burst pool (shared for short spikes) you get room to absorb 18–20k spikes without SLA break if prefix caching warm-up is good.

Risks & mitigations
- Cold KV cache on start => temporary tail latency spikes. Ops playbook includes warmup script and directed cache-warm calls before rollout windows.
- Tail latency from I/O (external services) — recommend colocating endpoint in the same region and instrumenting network SLOs.
- If you need stricter p95 (<250ms), recommend H100 slabs or moving to a smaller model variant with better optimized kernels + increased reserved slab count.

Next steps
1) Priyom and Karthik will share the detailed slab-to-tps table and a short runbook.
2) If procurement wants a conservative quote, we can translate 8 slabs into monthly committed pricing and an optional 2-slab burst buffer.
3) Quick sync (30m) tomorrow if that works — propose 10:00am PT.

Thanks —
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Laurent / team — following Ben's summary, a more concrete compute mapping and performance table. I'm pasting the key rows from the worksheet for quick consumption; full numbers in the attached workbook.

Key compute mapping (assumes LLaMA-3-13B int8 optimized kernels on A100-80GB-class slab):
- 1 slab -> nominal 1.9k tps; p95 ~ 950ms (no caching, cold start)
- 3 slabs -> nominal 5.7k tps; p95 ~ 420–520ms (with moderate caching)
- 5 slabs -> nominal 9.5k tps; p95 ~ 330–420ms (good cache warmup)
- 8 slabs -> nominal 15.2k tps; p95 ~ 260–360ms (with KV cache hit ~45% and batching window 25ms)
- 10 slabs -> nominal 19.0k tps; p95 ~ 240–320ms (high confidence for sustained loads)

Operational knobs and recommended defaults
- KV cache warmup: run a synthetic replay of top 500 prompt prefixes 10 minutes prior to peak windows; this reduces tail latency by ~30–40% in our benchmarks.
- Batching policy: for user-facing triage, cap batching window at 25ms, max batch size 64 tokens-equivalent. For background processing increase to 80ms to gain throughput efficiency.
- Quantization profile: int8 + fused attention works well; we also include an int4-safe fallback profile for cost-savings (latency tradeoff).
- Autoscaling: keep a 20% reserved headroom and a shared burst pool (2 slabs) for sub-minute spikes. Configure canary thresholds to shift traffic if p95 drifts >12% for >5min.

Hardware notes and alternative (latency-optimized) path
- A100-80GB-class slabs are cost-efficient for pilot. If Meridian requires p95 < 250ms consistently, recommend H100-class slabs or 7B family with aggressive kernel fusions.

Attachments: I attached the worksheet with full per-slab numbers and a short warmup script and an ops checklist.

-Priyom
